metric_rationale: This metric evaluates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Take The Best (TTB) prediction. Because the experimental design explicitly pits TTB against Tallying (creating multiple trials where the highest valid cue points to one option, but a larger number of lower-validity cues point to the other), TTB simulated data will score near 1.0 on this metric. Conversely, Tallying simulated data will systematically choose the opposite option on the mismatch trials, scoring very low (close to 0.0 or 0.1). This creates a massive, reliable gap with low between-subject variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of subject responses that align with the deterministic prediction of the Tallying heuristic, excluding trials where Tallying predicts a tie. Because the experimental design explicitly pits Tallying against Take The Best (TTB) by including many trials where a single high-validity cue points one way while a majority of lower-validity cues point the other way, the two models make strictly opposite predictions on most trials. Consequently, data generated under Tallying will yield a high value on this metric (reflecting high agreement), whereas data generated under TTB will yield a low value (reflecting choices driven by the single highest-validity cue rather than the unweighted majority). The averaging across a large number of discriminating trials per subject ensures low within-theory variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses Option A on 'compensatory' trials (Trials 1 and 2). On these trials, Option A possesses only the single highest-validity cue available, while Option B possesses all remaining lower-validity cues. The Take The Best (TTB) strategy will deterministically choose Option A because it bases its decision exclusively on the single best discriminating cue. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy will aggregate the evidence from the lower-validity cues, which together outweigh the single best cue for most values of the gamma parameter, thus leading WADD to predominantly choose Option B. Consequently, this metric will be close to 1 for TTB and much closer to 0 for WADD.

On Trial 1, Option A is favored by the single best cue (validity 0.95), while Option B is favored by all other cues (validities 0.9, 0.85, 0.8, 0.75). Take The Best will deterministically choose Option A (response 0) because it only considers the first discriminating cue. Weighted Additive, on the other hand, will integrate all cues and, for most values of gamma, strongly favor Option B (response 1) because the sum of the remaining validities outweighs the first. Measuring the proportion of B choices on this specific trial provides a highly stable and strongly discriminative metric between the two theories.

Previous metrics failed because the raw difference in TTB consistency (P_tie - P_extreme) has a variance that heavily depends on the subject's baseline noise level. Noisy subjects produce large variance but zero signal, diluting the metric's power. By computing the z-score (standardized difference in proportions) with Laplace smoothing, we divide the difference by the subject's standard error. For the pure TTB model, this z-score follows a standard normal distribution N(0, 1) regardless of the subject's noise level, tightly bounding the between-subject variance to ~1.0. For the mixture model, deterministic subjects (who have a large true difference and small standard error) yield massive z-scores, drastically amplifying the signal. This statistically optimal contrast maximizes the t-statistic between the two theories.

Pure Take The Best (TTB) predicts a constant probability of choosing Option A across all five trial types, because the most valid cue always favors Option A. The Mixture theory, however, predicts that as the number of lower-validity cues favoring Option B decreases from 5 (in trial 1) to 1 (in trial 5), the Tallying strategy will increasingly favor Option A. This metric computes the difference in the proportion of times Option A is chosen between trial 5 and trial 1. It will be near zero for Pure TTB and significantly positive for the Mixture model.

The experimental design contains specific trials where the single highest-validity discriminating cue favors Option A, but all remaining lower-validity cues favor Option B. Take The Best (TTB) ignores the lower-validity cues and deterministically chooses A. Probabilistic Cue Integration (WADD) integrates all available evidence, and because the sum of evidence from the lower-validity cues outweighs the single highest cue, it will typically choose B. By isolating these specific disagreement trials and calculating the proportion of times Option A is chosen, we get a metric that is near 1 for TTB and near 0 for WADD, providing maximal discrimination between the two theories.

The experimental design was specifically crafted such that Probabilistic Cue Integration (WADD) and Take The Best (TTB) make diametrically opposed predictions on every single trial type. TTB relies solely on the highest-validity discriminating cue, whereas WADD integrates all cues, allowing multiple lower-validity cues to outvote a single high-validity cue. This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the WADD prediction. Data generated by WADD will yield values near 1.0, while data generated by TTB will yield values near 0.0, maximally discriminating the two theories.

In all 5 trial types, the pure Take The Best (TTB) strategy favors Option A because the most valid discriminating cue always points to A. Therefore, TTB predicts a flat, low probability of choosing Option B across all trials (driven only by noise/lapses). However, the WADD strategy favors Option B in trials 1, 2, and 4, and favors Option A in trials 3 and 5. The competing mixture model incorporates WADD and thus predicts a systematically higher probability of choosing Option B on trials 1, 2, and 4 compared to trials 3 and 5. By measuring the difference in the proportion of B choices between these two sets of trials, we can cleanly separate the flat line of TTB from the WADD-influenced shifts of the mixture model.

In a pure Take The Best (TTB) model, the probability of choosing the option favored by the top discriminating cue is constant across all trials, regardless of the lower-validity cues. In the Advocated Theory's mixture model, the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy influences the choice. By calculating the difference in the rate of choosing the TTB-favored option between trials where WADD supports TTB (positive WADD difference) and trials where WADD opposes TTB (negative WADD difference), we can measure the compensatory influence. This metric will be near zero for the pure TTB model and significantly greater than zero for the Advocated mixture model.

Under Take The Best, only the first discriminating cue matters and its validity magnitude is ignored. Since both Trial 3 (A=11111, B=00000) and Trial 1 (A=10000, B=01111) are decided by the first cue favoring option A, TTB predicts an identical probability of choosing A in both trials, meaning the difference should be 0. The Competing Theory, however, accumulates evidence across all cues: in Trial 3, A is supported by all cues, while in Trial 1, B is strongly supported by the remaining four cues, making the probability of choosing A significantly lower in Trial 1. The metric computes the difference in the empirical probability of choosing A between these two trials.

TTB predicts identical choice probabilities for Trial 1 and Trial 3 because the first cue discriminates in favor of Option A in both cases, leading it to ignore all subsequent cues. The Advocated Theory accumulates evidence dynamically, predicting a significantly higher probability of choosing Option A in Trial 3 (where additional cues also favor A) compared to Trial 1 (where all lower cues strongly oppose A). The difference in the proportion of choosing A between Trial 3 and Trial 1 should be near zero for TTB, but strictly positive for the Advocated Theory.

In the experimental design, the number of features favoring Option A increases from 1 to 5 across the five trial types, while the highest-validity cue always favors Option A. The pure Take The Best (TTB) model ignores all but the highest-validity cue, predicting a flat probability of choosing Option A across all trials (covariance = 0). The Competing Theory (TTB + Tallying) incorporates the total number of features favoring each option, predicting a monotonic increase in the probability of choosing Option A as the tally shifts in its favor. By computing the covariance between the number of features favoring Option A and the binary choice (1 for A, 0 for B), we can reliably capture this monotonic trend using all available trials, reducing per-subject variance.

In the experimental design, pure Take The Best (TTB) consistently favors Option A across all trials because the highest validity discriminating cue always favors A. Therefore, pure TTB predicts no difference in the probability of choosing A between Trial 3 and Trial 1. However, the Advocated Theory incorporates Tallying. In Trial 3, Tallying strongly favors A (3 cues to 1), whereas in Trial 1, Tallying strongly favors B (3 cues to 1). The metric calculates the difference in the proportion of choosing Option A between Trial 3 and Trial 1. Pure TTB predicts a difference of 0, while the Advocated Theory predicts a positive difference.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing Option B between trials where Option B has many positive features (sum >= 3) and trials where it has few positive features (sum <= 1). According to the pure Take The Best (TTB) model, lower-validity cues are completely ignored when a higher-validity cue discriminates, meaning the number of positive features Option B has should not affect the choice probability. Thus, TTB predicts a difference of 0. In contrast, the Exponential Decay weighting model integrates all cues, so giving Option B more positive features increases its overall value and makes it more likely to be chosen, predicting a strictly positive difference.

In every trial of the experimental design, the highest-validity discriminating cue always favors Option A. Therefore, the Take The Best (TTB) model predicts a constant probability of choosing A across all trials, completely ignoring the lower-validity cues. In contrast, the Advocated Theory integrates all cues, so the probability of choosing A should increase as the number of lower-validity cues favoring A increases. This metric calculates the difference in the rate of choosing Option A between trials where the total number of features favors A (x > 0) versus trials where the total number of features favors B (x < 0). TTB predicts a difference of 0, whereas the Advocated Theory predicts a positive difference.

This metric calculates the difference in the proportion of choosing Option A between Trial 4 and Trial 1. In both trials, the most valid cue (Feature 1) favors Option A. Pure Take The Best (TTB) uses only this first cue, ignoring the rest, and thus predicts an identical probability of choosing A across both trials (difference around 0). However, the Competing Theory's mixture model incorporates a Tallying component. In Trial 1, Tallying strongly favors B (4 features to 1), whereas in Trial 4, Tallying strongly favors A (4 features to 1). Therefore, the mixture model predicts a substantially higher rate of choosing A in Trial 4 compared to Trial 1, resulting in a large positive difference.

The pure Take The Best (TTB) model predicts that choice probability is determined entirely by the first discriminating cue. In both Trial 1 and Trial 4, the highest-validity cue (Feature 1) strongly favors Option A, and thus pure TTB predicts an identical rate of choosing Option A across these two trials (a difference of 0). Conversely, the Advocated Theory (TTB-Tallying mixture) predicts that subjects will sometimes use a Tallying strategy. In Trial 1, Tallying strongly favors Option B (1 vs 4 positive features), while in Trial 4, Tallying strongly favors Option A (5 vs 0 positive features). Therefore, the mixture model predicts a substantially higher rate of choosing Option A in Trial 4 compared to Trial 1. This metric calculates exactly this difference: P(Choose A | Trial 4) - P(Choose A | Trial 1).

This metric calculates the difference in the proportion of choices for Option A between Trial 5 (where all cues favor A) and Trial 1 (where the most valid cue favors A but all other cues favor B). The pure Take The Best (TTB) model ignores lower-validity cues entirely once the highest-validity cue discriminates, thus predicting no difference (a value around 0). In contrast, the Sequential Evidence Accumulation model integrates evidence from lower-validity cues, predicting a much higher probability of choosing Option A in Trial 5 than in Trial 1, leading to a large positive value.

The Advocated Theory (Sequential Evidence Accumulation) predicts that as lower-validity cues increasingly favor Option A over Option B (moving from Trial 1 to Trial 7), the probability of choosing Option A will monotonically increase. The Competing Theory (Take The Best) predicts that because the highest-validity cue always favors Option A across all trials, decisions will be based solely on this first cue, resulting in a flat, identical probability of choosing Option A across all trials. Therefore, the difference in the probability of choosing A between Trial 7 and Trial 1 should be near zero for Take The Best, but significantly positive for Sequential Evidence Accumulation.

Previous attempts failed because they either averaged over weakly discriminating trials (diluting the effect) or used incorrect feature sums that resulted in empty trial slices. This metric perfectly isolates the two most extreme trials in the design: Trial 4 (where the compensatory WADD strategy overwhelmingly favors Option A) and Trial 1 (where WADD overwhelmingly favors Option B). Pure Take The Best predicts exactly the same probability of choosing Option A in both trials, as the highest-validity cue points to A in both cases, yielding an expected difference of 0. The Strategy Mixture Model predicts a massive shift in preference across these two trials, resulting in a large positive difference and cleanly discriminating the theories.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 5 (where all cues favor A) and Trial 1 (where only the most valid cue favors A, and all other cues favor B). According to the pure Take The Best (TTB) model, the decision is based solely on the first discriminating cue, which favors A in both trials; thus, TTB predicts this difference will be exactly zero. In contrast, the Strategy Mixture Model predicts that the compensatory Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy will strongly favor Option B in Trial 1 and Option A in Trial 5. Consequently, the Mixture Model predicts a significantly positive difference, cleanly discriminating the two theories.

Under the pure Take The Best (TTB) model, the probability of choosing Option A is constant across all trials where the first feature favors A, regardless of how many lower-validity cues contradict it. Thus, the difference in preference for A between low-contradiction trials (where B has 0-2 positive features) and high-contradiction trials (where B has 6-7 positive features) should be zero. In contrast, the Confirmatory Search model predicts a drop in the probability of choosing A once the number of contradicting cues exceeds a threshold, leading to a positive difference between these two sets of trials.

Under the Competing Theory (pure Take The Best), Option A wins on the highest validity cue in all trials, and lower validity cues are never consulted. Thus, the probability of choosing Option B is purely driven by response noise and remains constant across all trial types. Under the Advocated Theory, the decision-maker performs a confirmatory check on the remaining cues. If the net contradiction exceeds a threshold (which ranges from 2 to 6 across subjects), confidence in Option A drops, increasing the probability of choosing B. By specifically comparing trials with a net contradiction >= 6 (which guarantees the threshold is exceeded for ALL subjects) against trials with a net contradiction of 0 (which guarantees the threshold is NEVER exceeded), we maximize the expected mean difference in choice probabilities between the two groups. This targeted contrast maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio and minimizes between-subject variance compared to broader groupings, leading to stronger discriminability.
